The **Mask of Agamemnon** is a gold funerary mask which was discovered at the Bronze Age site of Mycenae in southern Greece. The mask, displayed in the National Archaeological Museum of Athens, has been described by the historian Cathy Gere as the "_Mona Lisa_ of prehistory".[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGere20111%E2%80%932-1)
German archaeologist Heinrich Schliemann, who discovered the artifact in 1876, believed that he had found the body of the Mycenaean king Agamemnon, leader of the Achaeans in the ancient Greek epic of the Trojan War, the _Iliad_. Modern archaeological research suggests that the mask dates to around the 16th century BC, pre-dating the period of the mythical Trojan War by 300–400 years.

Heinrich Schliemann found the gold funeral mask in 1876 in a shaft tomb designated Grave V, at the site Grave Circle A, Mycenae.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-Harrington1999-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-Gates2003-3) A total of eight men were discovered in Grave Circle A,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-Gates2003-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-Komita1982-4) all of whom had weapons in their graves,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-5) but only five had masks; those were in Grave IV and Grave V.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-Harrington1999-2)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-Komita1982-4)
The quantities of gold and carefully worked artifacts indicate honor, wealth and status. The Mask of Agamemnon was named by Schliemann after the legendary Greek king Agamemnon of Homer's _Iliad_. Schliemann took this as evidence the Trojan War was a real historical event.
Portrait of Heinrich Schliemann

The Mask of Agamemnon was created from a single thick gold sheet, heated and hammered against a wooden background with the details chased on later with a sharp tool.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-6) Following his discoveries at the site, Schliemann notified King George I.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-7) He is supposed to have told the king in a telegraph, "I have gazed upon the face of Agamemnon".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-8) Schliemann later named his son after the legendary king. Close to the end of his life, the archaeologist accepted doubts as to the mask's true owner and is quoted as saying, "So this is not Agamemnon... these are not his ornaments? All right, let's call him Schulze."[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-9)
The mask in the National Archaeological Museum
In the latter half of the 20th century and the beginning of the 21st century, the authenticity of the mask has been formally questioned, primarily by William Calder III and David Traill.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGere2011176-10)_Archaeology_ magazine has run a series of articles presenting both sides of the debate.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-11) By the time of the excavation of the Shaft Graves, the Greek Archaeological Society had taken a hand in supervising Schliemann's work (after the issues at Troy), sending Panagiotis Stamatakis as _ephor_, or director, of the excavation, who kept a close eye on Schliemann.
Proponents of the fraud argument center their case on Schliemann's reputation for salting digs with artefacts from elsewhere. The resourceful Schliemann, they assert, could have had the mask manufactured on the general model of the other Mycenaean masks and found an opportunity to place it in the excavation.

The defending advocate(s) point out that the excavation was closed on November 26–27 for Sunday holiday and rain. It was not allowed to reopen until Stamatakis had provided the work with credible witnesses. The three other masks were not discovered until the 28th. The Mask of Agamemnon was found on the 30th.
A second critique is based on style. The Mask of Agamemnon differs from three of the other masks in a number of ways: it is three-dimensional rather than flat, one of the facial hairs is cut out, rather than engraved, the ears are cut out, the eyes are depicted as both open and shut, with open eyelids, but a line of closed eyelids across the center, the face alone of all the depictions of faces in Mycenaean art has a full pointed beard with handlebar moustache, the mouth is well-defined (compared to the flat masks), the brows are formed to two arches rather than one.
The defense presented prior arguments that the shape of the lip, the triangular beard and the detail of the beard are nearly the same as the mane and locks of the gold lion-head rhyton from Shaft Grave IV. Schliemann's duplicity, they claim, has been greatly exaggerated, and they also claim that the attackers were conducting a vendetta.
Modern archaeological research suggests that the mask is genuine but pre-dates the period of the Trojan War by 300–400 years.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-12) Others date the contents of the find even earlier, to around 2500 BC.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-13)

“Mask of Agamemnon” in Athens’ National Archaeological Museum (Photo by Don Knebel)
Athens’ National Archaeological Museum is one of the world’s greatest museums, exhibiting 11,000 items that showcase Greek civilizations from prehistory to late antiquity. Its most celebrated, as well as most controversial, possession is a death mask discovered by German archaeologist Heinrich Schliemann that has been called the “Mona Lisa of prehistory.”   
Schliemann was the most famous archaeologist of the nineteenth century, known as much for his self-promotion, sometime based on outright falsehoods, as for his archaeological discoveries. He is best known for having uncovered what he claimed was the legendary City of Troy, the site of the Trojan War made famous by the Iliad. Convinced that Homer’s epic poem was based on actual events, Schliemann set out to find the tomb of Agamemnon, the mythical King of Mycenae who commanded the victorious Greek forces against the Trojans and was murdered upon his return by his wife’s lover. In 1876, while digging at Mycenae, Schliemann found five well-preserved male bodies, the face of each covered by a mask. The most elaborate of the masks, made from a sheet of gold hammered over a wooden mold, showed a bearded man with his eyes appearing both open and closed. The ears were cut out to allow the mask to be fastened to the head with string. Claiming the mask resembled an illustration of Agamemnon, Schliemann told the King of Greece he had gazed into the face of the legendary king.
Some skeptics, influenced by Schliemann’s truth problems, claimed he forged the mask from the illustration and planted it at the excavation site. However, most scholars believe the so-called “Mask of Agamemnon” is authentic, but fashioned in about 1500 B.C., 300 years before the reckoned date of the Trojan War and 200 years before the famous gold of Tutankhamen. Whether Agamemnon existed remains a mystery.

The first national archaeological museum in Greece was established in 1829. Subsequently, the archaeological collection was relocated to a number of exhibition places until 1858, when an international architectural competition was announced for the location and the architectural design of the new museum.The current location was proposed and the construction of the museum's building began in 1866 and was completed in 1889.
During World War II the museum was closed and the antiquities were sealed in special protective boxes and buried, in order to avoid their destruction and looting. It reopened in 1945.
I was fortunate to visit the museum early today, our last full day in the city. The place, only partially opened in the winter months is truly overwhelming.
One of its most celebrated and oldest artefacts is the Mask of Agamemnon. It is a gold funerary mask discovered at the Bronze Age site of Mycenae in southern Greece. Modern archaeological research suggests that the mask dates to about the 16th century BC and it has been described by the historian Cathy Gere as the "Mona Lisa of prehistory"
The Mask of Agamemnon was created from a single thick gold sheet, heated and hammered against a wooden background with the details chased on later with a sharp tool.

The defense presented prior arguments that the shape of the lip, the triangular beard and the detail of the beard are nearly the same as the mane and locks of the gold lion-head rhyton from Shaft Grave IV. Schliemann's duplicity, they claim, has been greatly exaggerated, and they also claim that the attackers were conducting a vendetta.
Modern archaeological research suggests that the mask is genuine but pre-dates the period of the Trojan War by 300–400 years.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-12) Others date the contents of the find even earlier, to around 2500 BC.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mask_of_Agamemnon#cite_note-13)

The first national archaeological museum in Greece was established in 1829. Subsequently, the archaeological collection was relocated to a number of exhibition places until 1858, when an international architectural competition was announced for the location and the architectural design of the new museum.The current location was proposed and the construction of the museum's building began in 1866 and was completed in 1889.
During World War II the museum was closed and the antiquities were sealed in special protective boxes and buried, in order to avoid their destruction and looting. It reopened in 1945.
I was fortunate to visit the museum early today, our last full day in the city. The place, only partially opened in the winter months is truly overwhelming.
One of its most celebrated and oldest artefacts is the Mask of Agamemnon. It is a gold funerary mask discovered at the Bronze Age site of Mycenae in southern Greece. Modern archaeological research suggests that the mask dates to about the 16th century BC and it has been described by the historian Cathy Gere as the "Mona Lisa of prehistory"
The Mask of Agamemnon was created from a single thick gold sheet, heated and hammered against a wooden background with the details chased on later with a sharp tool.

“Mask of Agamemnon” in Athens’ National Archaeological Museum (Photo by Don Knebel)
Athens’ National Archaeological Museum is one of the world’s greatest museums, exhibiting 11,000 items that showcase Greek civilizations from prehistory to late antiquity. Its most celebrated, as well as most controversial, possession is a death mask discovered by German archaeologist Heinrich Schliemann that has been called the “Mona Lisa of prehistory.”   
Schliemann was the most famous archaeologist of the nineteenth century, known as much for his self-promotion, sometime based on outright falsehoods, as for his archaeological discoveries. He is best known for having uncovered what he claimed was the legendary City of Troy, the site of the Trojan War made famous by the Iliad. Convinced that Homer’s epic poem was based on actual events, Schliemann set out to find the tomb of Agamemnon, the mythical King of Mycenae who commanded the victorious Greek forces against the Trojans and was murdered upon his return by his wife’s lover. In 1876, while digging at Mycenae, Schliemann found five well-preserved male bodies, the face of each covered by a mask. The most elaborate of the masks, made from a sheet of gold hammered over a wooden mold, showed a bearded man with his eyes appearing both open and closed. The ears were cut out to allow the mask to be fastened to the head with string. Claiming the mask resembled an illustration of Agamemnon, Schliemann told the King of Greece he had gazed into the face of the legendary king.
Some skeptics, influenced by Schliemann’s truth problems, claimed he forged the mask from the illustration and planted it at the excavation site. However, most scholars believe the so-called “Mask of Agamemnon” is authentic, but fashioned in about 1500 B.C., 300 years before the reckoned date of the Trojan War and 200 years before the famous gold of Tutankhamen. Whether Agamemnon existed remains a mystery.

The National Archaeological Museum is the largest museum in Greece and one of the most important museums of antiquities in the world: more than 11,000 exhibits across 8,000 m², from the Neolithic era to late antiquity. It is also the museum closest to Angel Athens — an 8-minute walk from Ioulianou 50. In this guide you'll find the 12 exhibits you shouldn't miss (with room numbers), three ready-made routes depending on your time, 2026 hours and tickets, directions (including wheelchair access), the café in the garden and a video tour to get a feel for the place before you go.

## 🏛️ The building and the garden
The museum occupies the imposing neoclassical building at **44 Patission (28is Oktovriou) Street**, between Victoria and Omonia, right next to the Polytechnic. The foundations were laid in 1866 on land donated by Eleni Tositsa, with funds from the Bernardakis family of St Petersburg, designs by Ludwig Lange and the final façade by Ernst Ziller. It opened its doors in 1889 and was extended eastwards in 1932–1939. In front of it stretches the garden with its palm trees and flower beds — one of the loveliest "courtyards" in Athens, where Polytechnic students and locals sit in the afternoons.
🏛️

## 🏛️ The building and the garden
### The National Archaeological Museum from outside
Ziller's façade, the garden and the entrance from Patission Street
1 / 5
The façade with the Ionic columns and the palms — the museum opened in 1889.

## 🎬 Video: a walk through the galleries
Before reading about the exhibits, see what the museum looks like inside. The video walks through the Prehistoric, Sculpture and Bronze galleries — you'll recognise several of the works below. Press play to load it (the video is only fetched from YouTube when you ask for it).
▶ Tour of the National Archaeological Museum of Athens · YouTube

## 🧭 Before you go in: how the museum is laid out
The museum is far too big for a casual stroll. You can easily spend half a day there and leave feeling you've only seen the beginning. It helps to know the logic of the building: on the **ground floor** are the Prehistoric Antiquities (rooms 3–6, directly opposite the entrance), Sculpture (rooms 7–35, in a loop around the building), the Bronzes (36–39) and the Egyptian Collection (40–41). On the **first floor** are the Thera frescoes (room 48), the Vase and Minor Arts Collection (49–63) and the Cypriot Collection (64).
Tip: start with the **Prehistoric Antiquities**. That's where the Mask of "Agamemnon", the Mycenaean finds and the Cycladic figurines are. Early in the morning the route is usually calmer and you can linger a little longer in front of the star pieces. Pick up the map at the entrance (or download the floor plans to your phone) — the room numbers below follow the official numbering.

## 🏆 The 12 exhibits you must not miss
### 1. The Mask of "Agamemnon"
📍 Room 4 · Ground floor · Mycenaean Collection · c. 1550–1500 BC
Heinrich Schliemann found it in a shaft grave at Mycenae in 1876 and immediately linked it to Agamemnon. The dating, however, places it about three centuries before the Trojan War as we know it from the epic tradition. The name stuck, but the mask is more interesting when you see it as a Mycenaean funerary object: thin gold sheet, closed eyes, a face that looks more like a ritual image than a portrait. In the same room, look at the other, less famous gold masks and the swords with gold inlay — the comparison says a lot.
1 / 2
The Mask of “Agamemnon”: a thin sheet of gold, eyes closed.
Photos: Jebulon (CC0), George E. Koronaios (CC BY-SA 4.0) · Wikimedia Commons

## 🏆 The 12 exhibits you must not miss
### 2. The royal tombs of Mycenae and the Vapheio Cups
📍 Rooms 3–4 · Ground floor · Mycenaean Collection · 16th–15th c. BC
In the same rooms you'll see gold cups, daggers with inlaid hunting scenes, libation vessels, seal stones and the famous "Warrior Vase" — objects that show wealth, technical mastery and contacts with the whole eastern Mediterranean of the Bronze Age. The two **Vapheio Cups**, with scenes of wild bulls being captured in gold relief, were found in a tholos tomb in Laconia and are considered among the finest examples of prehistoric Aegean metalwork. Take your time: the details are tiny.
1 / 3
A Vaphio cup: a wild bull caught in a net.
Photos: Zde (CC BY-SA 3.0), Sharon Mollerus (CC BY 2.0) · Wikimedia Commons

## 🏆 The 12 exhibits you must not miss
### 3. Cycladic figurines and the "Harpist" of Keros
📍 Room 6 · Ground floor · Cycladic Collection · 3200–2000 BC
The marble Cycladic figurines are small, austere and far more sophisticated than they look at first glance — it's no accident that they inspired Modigliani, Brancusi and Picasso. Look for the **"Harpist"**, a seated male figure playing a triangular harp, and the large female figurine from Amorgos, 1.5 metres tall. This room is a good, quiet breather before you move on to the sculpture.
1 / 2
The “Harpist” of Keros, seated with his harp.
Photos: Zde (CC BY-SA 4.0), Prof saxx (CC BY-SA 3.0) · Wikimedia Commons

## 🏆 The 12 exhibits you must not miss
### 4. The Akrotiri frescoes from Thera
📍 Room 48 · First floor · Thera Collection · c. 1600 BC

## 🏆 The 12 exhibits you must not miss
### Akrotiri on Thera: the "Pompeii of the Aegean"
The eruption of the Thera volcano buried the prehistoric town of Akrotiri under volcanic ash, preserving wall paintings of unusual vividness. The "Boxing Children", the "Antelopes" and the "Spring" fresco with its lilies and swallows show an Aegean world that is colourful, maritime and far more familiar than you'd expect from the Bronze Age. The room is dark and cool — a perfect stop on hot days.
1 / 2
“Spring”: lilies and swallows on every wall of a room.
Photos: Jebulon (CC0), ArchaiOptix (CC BY-SA 4.0) · Wikimedia Commons

## 🏆 The 12 exhibits you must not miss
### 5. Linear B tablets
📍 Room 5 · Ground floor · Mycenaean Collection · 1450–1200 BC
Small clay tablets, some no bigger than a credit card, inscribed with the earliest deciphered Greek script: a syllabic system used for accounting records in the Mycenaean palaces of Pylos, Mycenae and Thebes. They survived by pure accident: the palaces burned, the unbaked clay was fired, and the bureaucratic notes endured. Michael Ventris's decipherment in 1952 pushed the history of the Greek language back by about 700 years.
1 / 2
Linear B tablets from Pylos, 13th century BC.
Photos: Zde (CC BY-SA 4.0), Sharon Mollerus (CC BY 2.0) · Wikimedia Commons

## ♿ Accessibility
*   **Accessible entrance:** a separate entrance on the **Vas. Irakleiou Street** side (the side street to the right of the façade). You reach it either by ramp from the front garden or directly from the Vas. Irakleiou pavement. The main entrance has steps.  
*   A **lift** connects the ground and first floors (priority for visitors with mobility impairments). The ground-floor galleries are level, with only a few small changes in height.  
*   A **wheelchair** can be requested from the entrance staff, subject to availability — best to phone ahead (+30 213 214 4800).  
*   **Accessible toilets** on the ground floor. Free WiFi and a cloakroom for backpacks (large backpacks must be checked in).  
*   The museum offers a digital virtual tour for people with mobility or hearing impairments, and organises touch tours for blind visitors by arrangement.  
*   **Admission:** free for disabled visitors and one companion, on presentation of the relevant document.

## ☕ The café in the garden: "O Kipos tou Mouseiou"
One of the best-kept secrets in the area: the museum café operates in the inner garden-patio, with tables under the trees, among ancient architectural fragments and planting renewed with 700 new plant species. Best of all: **entry to the café is free, no ticket required** — you go in through the secondary entrance to the right of the main staircase. It keeps museum hours, with extended hours in the summer months.
☕

## ☕ The café in the garden: "O Kipos tou Mouseiou"
### O Kipos tou Mouseiou (The Museum Garden)
Coffee, light food and wine under the trees — no ticket needed
1 / 3
The tables in the garden — one of the quietest corners of central Athens.
On the menu: specialty espresso and freddo, fresh juices, salads, sandwiches, pies and small plates, Greek wines by the glass. Prices are reasonable for a museum (coffee €3–4, plates €7–14). The space hosts art exhibitions and music evenings during Ministry of Culture events — International Museum Day, the August Full Moon, European Heritage Days. We wrote about the café in detail in O Kipos tou Mouseiou: coffee in the garden of the National Archaeological Museum.

## 🛍️ The museum shop
The museum shop reopened, renovated and under new management, in August 2025 and keeps the museum's days and hours. You'll find the museum's official publications and catalogues, faithful replicas of exhibits (Cycladic figurines, the Mask of Agamemnon in various sizes, the Antikythera Mechanism), jewellery inspired by the collection and quality souvenirs — a far better choice than the tourist shops of Plaka for a gift with meaning.

## ⏳ How much time to allow — 3 ready-made routes
#### 90 minutes — the highlights
Mask of Agamemnon (room 4) → Cycladic (6) → Kouros of Sounion (8) → Zeus/Poseidon (15) → Jockey (21) → Marathon Boy (28) → Antikythera Mechanism (38). All on the ground floor, in a logical order.

“I have gazed upon the face of Agamemnon,” boasted **Heinrich Schliemann, the famous amateur archaeologist** who first unearthed the gold funeral mask at Mycenae in 1876.
Imagine his excitement and joy as he carefully brushed away the dirt to reveal the mask, depicting the face of a bearded man, glinting in the sunlight. But did it really belong to the king of Homeric legend?
Schliemann discovered the mask, still fastened to its corpse, in **Shaft Grave V of Grave Circle A, immediately south of the Lion Gate**, the main entrance of the Bronze Age citadel in the Greek Argolid. It was one of seven death masks discovered in the same grave circle, alongside an enormous cache of gold artifacts, inlcuding ornate weapons, staffs, jewelry, and ceremonial cups.
Ever his own best publicist and exercising a blind faith in the Homeric epics, Schliemann made the extraordinary claim that he had found the remains of **Agamemnon, the legendary Mycenaean ruler**, in a telegraph to King George of Greece.
Agamemnon’s exploits as the commander-in-chief of the Greek army at Troy were immortalized in **Homer’s _Iliad_**. He was murdered upon his return from the war by Aegisthus, the lover of his wife Clytemnestra – the story of the Aeschylus’ tragic play “Agamemnon,” written in the 5th century BC.
Schliemann undoubtedly used the death mask to generate media interest in his excavations at the Bronze Age site, but it’s _extremely_ unlikely that it belonged to the Homeric hero, if indeed Agamemnon ever existed as a historical figure.
Scale model of Mycenae. Grave Circle A is located to the right after the Lion Gate, the main entrance of the Bronze Age citadel.
What we do know is that Schliemann, who retired from commercial activities a multi-millionaire at the age of 36, was **a fanatical devotee of Homer, dedicating the rest of his life to proving the historicity of the _Iliad_ and the _Odyssey_**. As such, he gained a reputation for “salting” his archaeological digs with bogus artifacts or objects taken from elsewhere to back up his claims.

His first quest took him to Hissarlik in northwest Turkey, in search of **the ancient citadel of Troy**. From 1870 to 1873, his excavations, inlcuding the discovery of **a large cache of gold artifacts dubbed “Priam’s Treasure,”** brought him both international fame and notoriety in equal measure, especially among the academic elite who criticised his heavy-handed methods.
In 1874, Schliemann embarked on excavations at Mycenae, the heavily fortified center that gives its name to **the Late Bronze Age culture of mainland Greece from c. 1600 to 1200 BC**. The discovery and subsequent publication of the spectacular contents of Grave Circle A, inlcuding the so-called “Mask of Agamemnon,” sparked a global media frenzy at the time, but not everyone was convinced.
Created from a single sheet of gold, heated and hammered against a wooden mold, **the mask differs in style from the other death masks of Mycenae**, lending support to the theory that Schliemann may have had it manufactured and surreptitiously placed in the shaft grave as part of an elaborate hoax. Proponents of this argument state that it is the only one in three-dimensional form as opposed to flat, with cut-out ears, a finely-detailed beard and handlebar moustache, conspicuously different to how men are depicted in Mycenaean art, and the eyebrows form two arches instead of one. It is also extremely well preserved compared to the others.
One of the other funeral masks from Grave Circle A at Mycenae, also dated to the 16th century BC, but quite different in style to the so-called "Mask of Agamemnon."
So, was it just a publicity stunt? Did Schliemann really fabricate the mask? Or was he simply letting his imagination get the better of him?
Towards the end of this life, Schliemann, accepting doubts about the authenticity of the mask’s true owner, famously conceded: “So this is not Agamemnon … these are not his ornaments? All right, let’s call him Schulze.” But **he certainly made no admission of fraud**.

Instead, modern archaeological research has tentatively dated the mask to **the second half of the 16th century BC, at least 300 years _before_ the Trojan War** of _Iliad_-fame. One study even dated it as far back as 2500 BC – the Early Helladic period of mainland Greece.
The majority of scholars today agree that **the gold mask is authentically Mycenaean, an exquisite example of the early repoussé (embossing) technique**, and likely belonged to a warrior king or someone of extreme wealth and importance in early Mycenaean culture. Interestingly, death masks like the ones found at Mycenae have not been found at any other site from the Mycenaean world. As such, the mystery surrounding their origins continues.
The iconic “Mask of Agamemnon,” even if it didn’t belong to the Homeric king, is nevertheless an extraordinary treasure of prehistoric Greek archaeology. It can be seen **on display in Room 4 of the National Archaeological Museum in Athens**, mounted centrally with the other gold masks from Grave Circle A, amid the spectacular Collection of Mycenaean Antiquities.

## 🏛️ The building and the garden
The museum occupies the imposing neoclassical building at **44 Patission (28is Oktovriou) Street**, between Victoria and Omonia, right next to the Polytechnic. The foundations were laid in 1866 on land donated by Eleni Tositsa, with funds from the Bernardakis family of St Petersburg, designs by Ludwig Lange and the final façade by Ernst Ziller. It opened its doors in 1889 and was extended eastwards in 1932–1939. In front of it stretches the garden with its palm trees and flower beds — one of the loveliest "courtyards" in Athens, where Polytechnic students and locals sit in the afternoons.

## 🧭 Before you go in: how the museum is laid out
The museum is far too big for a casual stroll. You can easily spend half a day there and leave feeling you've only seen the beginning. It helps to know the logic of the building: on the **ground floor** are the Prehistoric Antiquities (rooms 3–6, directly opposite the entrance), Sculpture (rooms 7–35, in a loop around the building), the Bronzes (36–39) and the Egyptian Collection (40–41). On the **first floor** are the Thera frescoes (room 48), the Vase and Minor Arts Collection (49–63) and the Cypriot Collection (64).
Tip: start with the **Prehistoric Antiquities**. That's where the Mask of "Agamemnon", the Mycenaean finds and the Cycladic figurines are. Early in the morning the route is usually calmer and you can linger a little longer in front of the star pieces. Pick up the map at the entrance (or download the floor plans to your phone) — the room numbers below follow the official numbering.

## 🏆 The 12 exhibits you must not miss
### 1. The Mask of "Agamemnon"
📍 Room 4 · Ground floor · Mycenaean Collection · c. 1550–1500 BC
Heinrich Schliemann found it in a shaft grave at Mycenae in 1876 and immediately linked it to Agamemnon. The dating, however, places it about three centuries before the Trojan War as we know it from the epic tradition. The name stuck, but the mask is more interesting when you see it as a Mycenaean funerary object: thin gold sheet, closed eyes, a face that looks more like a ritual image than a portrait. In the same room, look at the other, less famous gold masks and the swords with gold inlay — the comparison says a lot.
1 / 2
The Mask of “Agamemnon”: a thin sheet of gold, eyes closed.

## 🏆 The 12 exhibits you must not miss
### 2. The royal tombs of Mycenae and the Vapheio Cups
📍 Rooms 3–4 · Ground floor · Mycenaean Collection · 16th–15th c. BC
In the same rooms you'll see gold cups, daggers with inlaid hunting scenes, libation vessels, seal stones and the famous "Warrior Vase" — objects that show wealth, technical mastery and contacts with the whole eastern Mediterranean of the Bronze Age. The two **Vapheio Cups**, with scenes of wild bulls being captured in gold relief, were found in a tholos tomb in Laconia and are considered among the finest examples of prehistoric Aegean metalwork. Take your time: the details are tiny.

A Vaphio cup: a wild bull caught in a net.

## 🏆 The 12 exhibits you must not miss
### 3. Cycladic figurines and the "Harpist" of Keros
📍 Room 6 · Ground floor · Cycladic Collection · 3200–2000 BC
The marble Cycladic figurines are small, austere and far more sophisticated than they look at first glance — it's no accident that they inspired Modigliani, Brancusi and Picasso. Look for the **"Harpist"**, a seated male figure playing a triangular harp, and the large female figurine from Amorgos, 1.5 metres tall. This room is a good, quiet breather before you move on to the sculpture.

## 🏆 The 12 exhibits you must not miss
### Akrotiri on Thera: the "Pompeii of the Aegean"
The eruption of the Thera volcano buried the prehistoric town of Akrotiri under volcanic ash, preserving wall paintings of unusual vividness. The "Boxing Children", the "Antelopes" and the "Spring" fresco with its lilies and swallows show an Aegean world that is colourful, maritime and far more familiar than you'd expect from the Bronze Age. The room is dark and cool — a perfect stop on hot days.

## 🏆 The 12 exhibits you must not miss
### 5. Linear B tablets
📍 Room 5 · Ground floor · Mycenaean Collection · 1450–1200 BC
Small clay tablets, some no bigger than a credit card, inscribed with the earliest deciphered Greek script: a syllabic system used for accounting records in the Mycenaean palaces of Pylos, Mycenae and Thebes. They survived by pure accident: the palaces burned, the unbaked clay was fired, and the bureaucratic notes endured. Michael Ventris's decipherment in 1952 pushed the history of the Greek language back by about 700 years.

## ♿ Accessibility
*   **Accessible entrance:** a separate entrance on the **Vas. Irakleiou Street** side (the side street to the right of the façade). You reach it either by ramp from the front garden or directly from the Vas. Irakleiou pavement. The main entrance has steps.

*   **Accessible toilets** on the ground floor. Free WiFi and a cloakroom for backpacks (large backpacks must be checked in).  
*   The museum offers a digital virtual tour for people with mobility or hearing impairments, and organises touch tours for blind visitors by arrangement.  
*   **Admission:** free for disabled visitors and one companion, on presentation of the relevant document.

## ☕ The café in the garden: "O Kipos tou Mouseiou"
One of the best-kept secrets in the area: the museum café operates in the inner garden-patio, with tables under the trees, among ancient architectural fragments and planting renewed with 700 new plant species. Best of all: **entry to the café is free, no ticket required** — you go in through the secondary entrance to the right of the main staircase. It keeps museum hours, with extended hours in the summer months.

Coffee, light food and wine under the trees — no ticket needed

The tables in the garden — one of the quietest corners of central Athens.
On the menu: specialty espresso and freddo, fresh juices, salads, sandwiches, pies and small plates, Greek wines by the glass. Prices are reasonable for a museum (coffee €3–4, plates €7–14). The space hosts art exhibitions and music evenings during Ministry of Culture events — International Museum Day, the August Full Moon, European Heritage Days. ## 🛍️ The museum shop
The museum shop reopened, renovated and under new management, in August 2025 and keeps the museum's days and hours. You'll find the museum's official publications and catalogues, faithful replicas of exhibits (Cycladic figurines, the Mask of Agamemnon in various sizes, the Antikythera Mechanism), jewellery inspired by the collection and quality souvenirs — a far better choice than the tourist shops of Plaka for a gift with meaning.

Mask of Agamemnon (room 4) → Cycladic (6) → Kouros of Sounion (8) → Zeus/Poseidon (15) → Jockey (21) → Marathon Boy (28) → Antikythera Mechanism (38). All on the ground floor, in a logical order.

#### 3 hours — recommended
All 12 exhibits at a relaxed pace, plus the Sculpture bonus, the Thera frescoes (48) and the vases on the first floor. Coffee break in the garden halfway through.

All six collections, including Egyptian and Cypriot, with lunch in the garden. Or split it over two visits — you're staying 8 minutes away.

## 💡 10 tips from Kathy
1.   **Go early or on a Tuesday afternoon.** Cruise-ship groups arrive between 10:30 and 13:00. At 08:30 you'll have the Mask almost to yourself.  
2.   **Start with the Prehistoric galleries (rooms 3–6)** and continue clockwise through Sculpture — that way you see the art in chronological order.  
3.   **Download the floor plans** (PDF from namuseum.gr) before you go in. The building is a labyrinth.  
4.   **Photography without flash is allowed** for personal use. No tripods or selfie sticks. Don't pose "imitating" the statues — staff will stop you.  
5.   **Large backpacks go to the cloakroom** (free). Take only your phone and water with you.  
6.   **Buy an e-ticket** at tickets.hh.gr to skip the queue, especially April–October.  
7.   **The café needs no ticket** — you can go just for a coffee in the garden, even on days you're not visiting the museum.  
8.   **With children:** aim for the Mechanism, the Jockey, the bronzes and the Egyptian mummies. One hour, then out for ice cream.  
9.   **Combine it** with a walk in Pedion tou Areos park (5 minutes) or along historic Patission Street.  
10.   **Check the temporary exhibitions** — they're often excellent and included in the ticket.

## 🏠 From Angel Athens
The National Archaeological Museum is the great advantage of staying in Victoria. From **Ioulianou 50** it's an 8-minute walk — no metro, no taxi — so you can split it into two visits, come back for coffee in the garden, or go on a Tuesday afternoon when the galleries empty out. In the morning, before the groups arrive, you're there within 10 minutes of getting out of bed.
